articles.title: George Washington once used New Jersey’s Ford Mansion as his wartime headquarters; after nearly 10 months of restoration, the historic house reopened for public tours in October 2024
articles.summary: Explore the newly restored Ford Mansion, George Washington's historic wartime headquarters, now open for public tours in Morristown, New Jersey, after extensive renovations.
articles.body: Balancing modern structural preservation with historical integrity remains a constant challenge in Morristown, New Jersey. The Ford Mansion’s fate was once decided by an auctioneer’s hammer. Fast forward 151 years, the house that sheltered George Washington during the Revolutionary War shut down for repairs and reopened on 5 October 2024.According to the National Park Service (NPS), the reopening followed nearly ten months of restoration. The work involved repainting the exterior, restoring historic windows, and repointing sections of the foundation. Each windowpane received ultraviolet-protective film, and new period-appropriate draperies were installed. The house was also given permanent silhouette figures, which the NPS calls “new visitors”. The reopening was announced on 26 September 2024, and work on the grounds was continuing.The mansion was built in the early 1770s for Jacob Ford Jr., an iron manufacturer and colonel in the Morris County Militia. Ford passed away in January 1777, when 35 Delaware soldiers were quartered there. His widow, Theodosia, later allowed Washington to use the family home.A family home used as a Wartime headquartersIn December 1779, Washington arrived and remained through the winter of 1779-80. The mansion had 12 rooms and was a Georgian-style residence. Theodosia and her four children occupied two rooms. The rest accommodated Washington, his wife Martha, five aides-de-camp, 18 servants, dignitaries, and, at times, guards.The winter was severe, and the NPS said the season brought more than 20 snowstorms. After Washington’s 6-month stay, the Ford family continued living in the house. It remained privately owned until the 1870s, when the death of its last private owner, Henry Augustus Ford, put its future up in the air. Following his will, the property was divided into lots and sold at auction to provide for his descendants.As per the NPS account of the Ford Mansion auction, the sale took place on 25 June 1873; 19 of the 47 lots were claimed, for a total of $44,310, excluding the headquarters property. When bidding for the mansion reached $24,100, former governor Thomas Randolph stepped forward with General Norris Halsted and George Halsey. But, according to the same account, they agreed to buy it for any sum up to $25,000 if a fourth person joined them, with each man receiving a quarter share. William Van Vleck Lidgerwood joined the group, and the house was sold to the four men for $25,000.From private purchaser to public toursThe purchasers intended to hold the property until New Jersey took it over, but the state did not assume ownership. They established the Washington Association of New Jersey, an association dedicated to preserving the residence and opening it to visitors. The house was described by the NPS as one of the earliest house museums in the United States.The association maintained the site until 1933. But growing attendance, more automobile travel, and financial pressure during the Great Depression made it difficult to keep it afloat. By 1931, a national historical park in Morristown was under consideration. The association’s trustees supported transferring the headquarters property, along with the Jockey Hollow and Fort Nonsense lands, into the National Park System. President Herbert Hoover signed the legislation on 3 March 1933. Subsequently, the association and the town handed over the deeds to Interior Secretary Harold Ickes on 4 July, the same year.The park furnished the mansion to make it look as close as possible to how it might have appeared during Washington’s stay. When the house reopened in October 2024, tours were scheduled for 11 am, 1 pm, 2 pm, and 3 pm, each lasting about 45 minutes. The groups in attendance were limited to 20 people and were admitted on a first-come, first-served basis.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: JBLM soldier sentenced to 70 years for Gorge Amphitheatre murders, assaults
articles.summary: A Joint Base Lewis-McChord soldier has been sentenced to 70 years in military prison after pleading guilty to killing two Seattle nurses and wounding three o...
articles.body:
A Joint Base Lewis-McChord soldier has been sentenced to 70 years in military prison after pleading guilty to killing two Seattle nurses and wounding three other people during a 2023 shooting at the Gorge Amphitheatre campground.

James M. Kelly , 29, faced a court-martial held at JBLM Nov. 2 through Nov. 5, 2026. According to the Army Office of Special Trial Counsel, Kelly pleaded guilty to the murders of Brandy Escamilla and Josilyn Ruiz , along with charges of domestic violence, reckless discharge of a firearm, and the wrongful use and possession of psilocybin

A military judge sentenced Kelly to 70 years in confinement, reduced his rank to E-1, and ordered his dishonorable discharge from the Army.

The shooting happened June 17, 2023, while Kelly and his girlfriend were attending the Beyond Wonderland music festival at the Gorge Amphitheatre near George.

According to the Army, Kelly ingested psilocybin and began displaying paranoid behavior. Court documents previously obtained by KIRO 7 said Kelly told investigators he began hallucinating and believed the world was ending. He and his girlfriend returned to their campsite, where Kelly retrieved a handgun from a locked box inside his truck.

Kelly then shot and killed Brandy Escamilla, 29, and Josilyn Ruiz, 26, as the couple passed near the campsite, according to the Army.

The Army said Kelly continued firing and shot a bystander in the shoulder. The wounded man, Andrew Cuadra of Eugene, later told KIRO 7 that he ran and hid behind a tent after being shot, thinking about his two young daughters as he tried to survive.

Prosecutors said Kelly then moved away from the campsite with his girlfriend. When she called 911 and attempted to intervene, Kelly assaulted her and shot her twice in the lower body.

Kelly also fired at an all-terrain vehicle carrying three security personnel responding to the shooting and shot at a law enforcement drone being used to locate him, according to the Army.

Police eventually shot and wounded Kelly, ending the attack. He was arrested and initially held in Grant County.

The shooting caused chaos across the campground and led organizers to cancel the festival's second day. Witnesses previously told KIRO 7 that people ran from the area as workers warned them about an active shooter.

In the months after the shooting, friends, relatives and members of the Seattle music community gathered at Cal Anderson Park for a candlelight vigil honoring Escamilla and Ruiz.

Escamilla and Ruiz were engaged, and both worked as nurses in Seattle. Ruiz was remembered by relatives for her love of helping others, music, dancing, travel, and snowboarding.

The Swedish Cancer Institute, where Escamilla worked as an oncology nurse, later installed a memorial engraved with both women's names . Coworkers remembered Escamilla for her compassion, humor, and ability to give patients hope.

In 2024, the victims' families filed a wrongful death lawsuit against Live Nation . The lawsuit alleged the company had policies prohibiting drugs and weapons at the festival but failed to enforce them.

The Army took over prosecution of the criminal case in February 2026 at the request of the Grant County Prosecuting Attorney's Office.

"This sentence reflects the seriousness of Spc. Kelly's conduct and represents an important step towards accountability and justice," Army prosecutor Capt. Stewart Miller said. "We will continue to honor the victims and their families, and hope this result brings a measure of closure to a long and tragic chapter in the many lives impacted by this case."

The investigation involved numerous local, state, and federal agencies, including the Washington State Patrol, Grant County Sheriff's Office, Moses Lake Police Department, and Army Criminal Investigation Division.

Kelly will serve his sentence at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

articles.title: Deadlocked jury continues its deliberations in Matthew Farwell trial
articles.summary: It was a stunning end Monday to the first full day of deliberations in the Matthew Farwell trial, with the jury already reporting that it’s deadlocked.
articles.body: It was a stunning end Monday to the first full day of deliberations in the Matthew Farwell trial, with the jury already reporting that it’s deadlocked. Deliberations continue Tuesday at the federal courthouse in Boston, but uncertainty remains. At the beginning of the day, Judge Denise Casper addressed the jury in response to the notes they sent her. She told them to take the time they need, explaining that the court does not have the ability to stay open past 6 p.m., but they are free to return day to day to complete their duty. She then sent them back to resume their deliberations. If that doesn’t work, she could take additional steps. A Tuey-Rodriguez charge is a special instruction given by a judge in Massachusetts to a deadlocked jury that is struggling to reach a unanimous verdict. It’s known as the “Allen charge” in federal court. NBC10 Boston chief legal analyst Michael Coyne explains it’s a supplemental instruction urging a jury to forego their differences and come to a unanimous decision. He said it’s not if the judge will do this but when. Coyne didn’t expect it to be first thing this morning. He points out this is not a traditional murder trial. Jurors who don’t believe Sandra Birchmore died by suicide are not just deciding did Farwell do it -- but they’re deciding if he did it to stop her from reporting his crimes to law enforcement. Jurors deliberated for a little more than three hours Friday before going home for the weekend. The former Massachusetts police officer is accused of killing a pregnant Birchmore to keep her from revealing he had begun sexually abusing her when she was 15. Federal prosecutors say Farwell killed Birchmore, 23, and tried to stage her death as a suicide on Feb. 1, 2021, after learning she was pregnant with what he thought was his child. At the time, Farwell was a married detective with the Stoughton Police Department, where Birchmore had participated in a youth program as a child. “You know on Feb. 1 Matthew Farwell didn’t go to Sandra Birchmore’s apartment for a clean break,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Brian Fogarty told the jury in closing arguments. “He went to clean up the mess he created for himself years earlier, a mess that could bring serious charges and destroy his life. He cleaned up the mess by taking Sandra’s life.” Lawyers for Farwell, who is now 40, acknowledge he had an extramarital relationship with Birchmore. But they say he didn’t kill her and didn’t have sex with her until she was old enough to consent under Massachusetts law. They said Birchmore had threatened suicide before and that she was devastated when Farwell came to her apartment to break up with her that February. “When all is lost and all hope is gone and you’re alone in the world, are you going to pick your phone up? Or did she sit down and take that strap and make the pain stop?” Farwell’s attorney, Kimberly Stevens, told the jury. The nearly monthlong trial — with about 50 witnesses and 500 exhibits — unfolded in federal court in Boston, partly because local prosecutors never brought criminal charges. Massachusetts State Police officers and investigators, some with personal connections to Farwell, quickly concluded Birchmore’s death was a suicide after she was found slumped on her apartment floor with a strap around her neck. One investigator, Fogarty said, saw nothing suspicious in Birchmore’s apartment and concluded this was a “troubled girl who killed herself.” The state’s medical examiner, relying partly on information from police, initially ruled Birchmore died by suicide. The office has since changed the official manner of death to “undetermined.” Birchmore’s friends and family never believed the teacher’s aide had killed herself. She had told dozens of friends about her pregnancy and, according to prosecutors, was thrilled to start her next chapter as a single mom. A stroller, still in the box, was found in her apartment along with an ultrasound photo pinned to her refrigerator. The FBI began looking into Birchmore’s death in 2023, partly at the urging of a former deputy chief at the Stoughton Police Department who had led an internal affairs investigation into Farwell. Federal investigators concluded the local probe was rushed and compromised. Farwell was interviewed for just 15 minutes in a parking lot, they said. Investigators didn’t take notes, examine him for injuries or sample his DNA. Police looked at Farwell’s phone only after he had deleted texts with Birchmore. The FBI investigation uncovered about 40,000 texts between Farwell and Birchmore, including some in which they reminisced about having sex when he was 27 and she was 15 — too young to consent under Massachusetts law. The texts also showed how their relationship grew contentious as Birchmore pressed Farwell to get her pregnant and threatened to tell his wife about their relationship. Prosecutors argued that Farwell also feared Birchmore would contact law enforcement about his crimes. He became more controlling, prosecutors said, tracking her phone and ordering her to delete compromising communications. Texts in late 2020, after she was pregnant, showed they argued over what role, if any, Farwell would play in the child’s life. A paternity test after Birchmore’s death revealed a different man was the father. Twelve days before she died, a friend of Birchmore had called the Stoughton Police Department to report their affair. A digital forensics expert testified that on the night of Birchmore’s death, her phone stopped moving three minutes before the lobby security camera recorded Farwell leaving her building. An expert hired by prosecutors, Dr. William Smock, testified that Birchmore’s injuries indicated she was strangled with a duffel bag strap and that she struggled before dying. He noted that her glasses were not near her body and a pair of flip-flops were overturned. A defense expert, Dr. Thomas Andrew, the former chief medical examiner in New Hampshire, dismissed Smock’s determination that it was a homicide.

articles.title: Seven in hospital after car 'mounts pavement' in Glasgow
articles.summary: Police said the driver was assessed by paramedics and treated at the scene of the incident, which happened at about 15:45 on Hyndland Road.
articles.body:
Seven people have been taken to hospital after they were struck by a car in the west end of Glasgow.

Police Scotland said the driver was assessed by paramedics and treated at the scene of the incident, which happened at about 15:45 on Hyndland Road.

Unconfirmed reports suggest the vehicle mounted the pavement, hit a bus stop shelter and then struck scaffolding before coming to a halt.

A force spokesperson said: "Officers remain in attendance and inquiries are ongoing into the incident which is being treated as a road traffic collision."

Hyndland Road remains closed and members of the public are urged to avoid the area.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said it sent two appliances to the scene.

One resident told BBC Scotland News that staff from a nearby doctor's surgery raced to help at the scene.

A dog walker said it was unusual to see so many police vehicles in the area and a local woman described the scale of the response as "quite scary".

First Minister John Swinney posted on social media that he was "deeply concerned" by the reports.

He added: "I want to thank the emergency services. My thoughts are with everyone affected and their loved ones."

Hyndland Road is currently closed to all traffic between Clarence Drive and Novar Drive.

articles.title: Iran backs nuclear treaty even as hardliners raise prospect of bomb
articles.summary: Iran says it is committed to non-proliferation treaty, but hardliners may be pushing for a change in nuclear policy.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iran says it has not suspended its commitments under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), but as mediated talks to end the war with the United States continue, broad international inspections of Iranian sites remain far off.

Following US and Israeli attacks on Iran’s main nuclear facilities in and assassinations of senior leaders, Iranian authorities have increasingly discussed the possibility of abandoning the international treaty and building a nuclear bomb.

US President Donald Trump’s threats to attack the underground Pickaxe Mountain complex near the Natanz nuclear facility and other sensitive sites have only emboldened hardliners in Tehran to demand a shift in the country’s nuclear doctrine – under assassinated Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, nuclear weapons were officially forbidden.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei emphasised to reporters during a news conference in Tehran on Monday that the Islamic Republic remains committed to the NPT, despite restricting cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog.

“Other parties have imposed conditions, namely the attacks by the US and Zionist regime against our nuclear facilities which have caused issues concerning implementation of safeguards commitments,” he said, in reference to Israel.

“As long as this situation continues, we cannot act like normal circumstances in our cooperation with the agency,” Baghaei said about the IAEA, while also renewing Tehran’s criticism of its director, Rafael Grossi.

But the spokesman confirmed that new IAEA inspections were conducted days earlier at the Bushehr nuclear power plant.

The electricity generation plant, built in cooperation with Russia and under development for new phases, is the only facility still accessible to the agency, as it was not directly bombed during the war. US warplanes did, however, attack the perimeter of the plant several times and caused damage, prompting partial evacuation of Russian personnel, who have yet to fully return.

IAEA chief Grossi told the UN Security Council in late October that the body was unable to verify Iran’s nuclear material because Tehran “has not provided the requested information and access”.

Ali Vaez, deputy director of the Middle East and North Africa programme at the International Crisis Group, said Tehran is keeping one foot inside the NPT and the other near the exit.

“Allowing inspections at Bushehr is a low-cost gesture designed to keep diplomacy alive and hardliners at bay, while preserving leverage over the underground nuclear sites that matter most,” he told Al Jazeera.

Those sensitive sites include the Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan facilities, among others.

Seyed Hossein Mousavian, a visiting researcher at Princeton University and a former Iranian nuclear negotiator, said Iran’s position “reflects a distinction between honouring its NPT commitments and permitting inspections of facilities that have been bombed”.

Mousavian said the IAEA had no established inspection protocol for nuclear facilities damaged by military attacks, and pointed out that the Iranians fear that IAEA access to sensitive sites would lead to information being shared with the US and Israel that could then be used in future attacks.

“Tehran views restrictions on broader inspections as a security concern rather than necessarily a rejection of its NPT obligations,” he said.

Iran has had one of the most scrutinised nuclear programmes in history, and its international obligations are governed by several treaties and UN resolutions.

The NPT establishes the fundamental rules against nuclear proliferation, while recognising the right to peaceful nuclear energy. A separate safeguards agreement with the IAEA sets out how the agency monitors Iran’s nuclear activities to make sure it isn’t moving towards weapons development. Subsidiary arrangements, UN Security Council resolutions and nuclear agreements have fulfilled additional requirements.

As a party to the NPT, Iran’s peaceful nuclear-use rights are recognised, and it is allowed to undertake peaceful exchanges and receive assistance with nuclear development.

In exchange, the country commits not to receive, manufacture or otherwise acquire nuclear weapons, and to accept safeguards and information sharing in its territory.

Withdrawal requires a notice after a decision has been made that “extraordinary events” have “jeopardised the supreme interests” of the country.

However, the treaty does not protect from conventional military attack, and this gap between promised peaceful-use benefits and actual vulnerability has been at the centre of the appeal by domestic hardliners to leave the NPT.

But such considerations have not been limited to a handful of hawkish figures.

Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has publicly deliberated the possibility of abandoning the treaty on multiple occasions. Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), said earlier this week that the organisation “will create the necessary preparations” if the Islamic Republic goes through with the decision to change its nuclear doctrine.

Regional mediators like Qatar and Pakistan continue to relay messages between Iran and the US to prevent another all-out war, although analysts have warned that escalation is likely over the coming months.

Tehran has maintained that it will not allow its highly enriched uranium to be taken out of the country, but remains open to downblending it under international supervision inside Iran. It has also said it will not abandon enrichment altogether, but can accept a limit on enrichment as it did with the 2015 nuclear deal that US President Donald Trump unilaterally abandoned in 2018, during his first term in office.

Arriving at a deal that thoroughly addresses Iran’s nuclear programme would also require a resolution to hostilities in the Strait of Hormuz and beyond, something that is unlikely to materialise in the foreseeable future.

“Tehran might be willing to open the door a crack in exchange for tangible American concessions, but it is unlikely to surrender its most valuable nuclear bargaining chips upfront,” the Crisis Group’s Vaez said.

The expert added that a preliminary deal could potentially unlock limited, phased inspections based on the 2025 Cairo agreement between Iran and the IAEA.

The agreement came several months after the US and Israel bombed Iran’s nuclear facilities during the 12-day war of June 2025. It envisaged restored access for agency inspectors to all Iranian facilities, if case-by-case permission is granted by the country’s Supreme National Security Council.

But it was never enforced, and was followed by tensions that led to the US and Israel attacking Iran again on February 28.

“Restoring meaningful transparency over Iran’s nuclear programme will require a larger bargain on enrichment, stockpiles and sanctions relief,” Vaez said.

But Mousavian said Tehran would want more than just a preliminary agreement like the Cairo deal.

“Such cooperation would require a comprehensive agreement that addresses the overall security and nuclear issues; without it, inspections of the bombed sites are unlikely,” he said.

articles.title: Cerys Matthews pays tribute to her family as she receives an OBE
articles.summary: Matthews was behind the Welsh rock band Catatonia who shot to fame during the "Cool Cymru" movement of the 1990s.
articles.body:
Singer and presenter Cerys Matthews paid tribute to her family as she received an OBE.

Matthews, from Cardiff, was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for services to music and received a medal from the Prince of Wales.

The 57-year-old hosts a BBC Radio 6 Music show every Sunday and was a founding member of Welsh rock band Catatonia who shot to fame during the 'Cool Cymru' movement of the 1990s.

Speaking after the ceremony, Matthews said she accepted the OBE in memory of her family and "in gratitude of the freedoms I have as a female in this era".

Matthews' voice is also familiar to many over her Christmas holidays because of her 1999 rendition of Baby It's Cold Outside, sung with Sir Tom Jones.

After the ceremony she said Prince William discussed Catatonia with her, adding he "evidently" was a fan.

Matthews wore Black Watch tartan – Scotland's royal regimental tartan – to the ceremony in memory of her grandfather Oswald, who served in World War Two and took part in the D-Day landings on the beaches of Normandy in 1944.

She said her grandmother, Olive, did not have the freedom to pursue music because of economic and societal barriers as a young, working-class wartime bride.

"I grew up in the 80s and 90s as a female who loved music, and I've been allowed, and I've thrived, in the music industry.

"Sharing other people's music and making my own, and I accept this honour in their memory, and in gratitude of the freedoms I have as a female in this era.

"This positive change… I hope it continues across the world."

Meanwhile, techno DJ Carl Cox received an OBE for services to music after being a major figure in the British dance music scene for more than four decades.

The Manchester-born artist said: "By next year, I would have been putting needle on the record for 50 years, so it's quite a thing to be able to still keep doing something, even at my time of my life as a 64-year-old man."

articles.title: A Pennsylvania woman said she used $80,000 in savings during marriage, including to improve her husband's house; after five years of temporary support, an appeals court upheld another $1,000 a month for three years
articles.summary: A Pennsylvania appeals court has upheld an order requiring a man to pay his former wife $1,000 (£770) per month in alimony for three years.
articles.body: A Pennsylvania appeals court has upheld an order requiring a man to pay his former wife $1,000 (£770) per month in alimony for three years. The court rejected his argument that the five years of temporary financial support he had already paid during their divorce proceedings was enough. The ruling by the Superior Court of Pennsylvania upheld a financial order issued after the divorce by the Adams County Court of Common Pleas in the case of Cathell v. Cathell, filed under case number 491 MDA 2026. According to official court records published on Justia Law, James D. Cathell appealed the lower court's decision to award monthly alimony to his former wife, Lisa M. Cathell. James argued that the couple had been married for eight years and that he had already paid temporary spousal support, known as alimony pendente lite (APL), for five years while the divorce case was ongoing. He said requiring him to pay another three years of alimony was unreasonable. However, the appeals court agreed with the lower court. The judges found that Lisa's financial contributions during the marriage and her reduced ability to earn money justified the continued monthly payments.Marital savings spent on husband's homeJames and Lisa Cathell married on 8 February 2012. They remained together for eight years before separating, according to court records. During their marriage, Lisa used around $80,000 (£61,500) from her personal retirement savings, which she had built up before the marriage. Court records show that she used the money to help pay household expenses and make improvements to a residential property owned solely by her husband. The trial court noted that Lisa had used up her life savings during the marriage. As a result, she had no retirement savings left when the divorce proceedings took place. When dividing the couple's marital assets, the Adams County court awarded Lisa 63 per cent of the total. Despite receiving this share, Lisa told the court during a hearing on 30 June 2025 that her financial situation had become much worse after the separation. "She explained that she was seeking alimony for support for the next couple of years because she was a housewife for most of her life and did not make a lot of money," the court memorandum stated. Lisa also told the court that she was living on a limited income and struggling to earn enough to pay for her basic needs.Appellate court dismisses husband's appealIn his appeal to the Superior Court, James argued that Lisa was able to work full-time and keep a job. He pointed out that she did not have any physical disability or medical condition that stopped her from working. James also argued that Lisa had already received 63 per cent of the marital assets and five years of temporary spousal support. He said that making him pay another three years of alimony would mean he had to provide financial support for a total of eight years, the same length as their marriage. The Superior Court judges reviewed the legal factors used by the lower court when deciding whether to award alimony. These factors include the financial needs of the person receiving support, the standard of living during the marriage, and the paying spouse's ability to afford the payments. The court's opinion also noted that the divorce hearing officer had concerns about James's credibility during his testimony. By comparison, Lisa's behaviour and presentation during the hearing were considered satisfactory. The judges concluded that the trial court had made the right decision by considering Lisa's financial needs alongside James's ability to pay."Regardless of that error, the record supports Wife's position that she has difficulty supporting herself more so than Husband," the Superior Court panel wrote in its decision upholding the Adams County court's order. The court also explained that under Pennsylvania family law, alimony payments can be changed in the future. articles.title: Spain braces for nationwide strike as anger over housing, costs boils over
articles.summary: The 24-hour walkout, called by Spain’s two biggest unions, is due to start on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Spain is bracing for a nationwide general strike over soaring rents and the cost of living, as a deepening housing crisis fuels social unrest weeks before a crucial election .

The 24-hour walkout due to begin at midnight on Wednesday was called by Spain’s two biggest unions – the Comisiones Obreras (CCOO) and Union General de Trabajadores (UGT) – under their slogan: wages, housing, prices. The last time the pair called a general strike was in 2012 when the country was engulfed in an austerity crisis.

The protest will disrupt transport, schools, healthcare and other public services across Spain. Flight cancellations and delays are also expected, while public transport in major cities will operate at reduced capacity.

Schools, hospitals, shops and other services could also face closures or reduced staffing, although minimum services will be maintained in essential sectors.

The action follows the September eviction of an 87-year-old, who has since passed away, from her home in Madrid, after her corporate landlord increased the rent. Images of Maricarmen Abascal being forcibly removed on a stretcher struck a nerve. The moment led to nationwide demonstrations and encampments in a wave of protests that also fuelled a political crisis, prompting the government to call the November 29 snap elections.

Wednesday’s strike could help the government bring the housing crisis back to the centre of the political debate, said Luke Stobart, a political analyst who writes about social movements and politics in Spain.

“(Socialist Prime Minister Pedro) Sanchez has been famous for taking risks in the past, and he’s often been quite successful when he’s taken them. And he knows that if you have a general strike before elections, that will force everyone to talk about housing. And that is happening – it is helping to keep housing at the centre of the debate in the run-up to the elections,” Stobart said.

The country has 750,000 fewer homes than it needs, according to the Bank of Spain, which estimates that the gap could exceed one million by 2028.

Rents have rocketed to an average of 1,176 euros ($1,318) per month, and the average salary of a young person is 1,190 euros ($1,333), according to data collated by the Spanish Youth Council.

Many struggling to make ends meet are forced to live in overcrowded shared flats or stay with their parents.

Spain is not alone, as other European nations witness weekly mass protests over costs and living conditions.

While Sanchez has not explicitly endorsed the strike, he praised collective action as the driving force behind the country’s social gains.

“Your eight-hour working day. Your pension. Your public healthcare. None of this fell from the sky. They were collective achievements. We will not let anyone take them away from us,” the prime minister said in a video message on Monday.

He believes his government has more to offer on social policies than political opponents.

But his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) has lost support in recent months over its handling of the migration crisis in Ceuta. It is also plagued by a series of corruption scandals involving Sanchez’s inner circle and family members.

Recently, a deadly train crash in early November gave the opposition, the conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox, an opportunity to shift the national debate towards transport safety and what they described as government incompetence.

The crash, which occurred on the same railway line as another deadly accident less than a year earlier, killed 69 people. Transport Minister Oscar Puente, a senior PSOE figure and close ally of Sanchez, resigned .

The PP is ahead in opinion polls and could form a government with Vox, a prospect that would bring a far-right party into Spain’s national government for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco’s 1939-1975 dictatorship.

Both opposition parties have dismissed the strike as politically motivated, accusing unions of targeting the opposition ahead of the election. They have also criticised its timing, coming a day after the state funeral for the victims of the train accident.

Stobart said the strike has multiple layers, with different left-leaning groups putting forward a different narrative.

Some are critical of the government. These include Basque unions ELA and LAB, Galicia’s CIG, and Spain’s CGT, which have accused the regional and national governments of failing to tackle housing speculation.

“It’s not clear whether the big trade union leaders and the government are going to be able to control the narrative,” Stobart said, warning that the protests could develop into a broader wave of social unrest, as seen in France and Italy, potentially backfiring on the government.

articles.title: Sophie Turner travelled to Rwanda to meet women who survived the genocide; the Game of Thrones actress later became an ambassador for an organisation helping survivors rebuild their lives
articles.summary: Sophie Turner, best known for playing Sansa Stark in Game of Thrones, used her experience on the television series to draw attention to sexual violence
articles.body: Sophie Turner, best known for playing Sansa Stark in Game of Thrones, used her experience on the television series to draw attention to sexual violence and the struggles faced by women survivors of conflict. In 2017, the British actress travelled to Rwanda, where she met women affected by the 1994 genocide and witnessed how they were rebuilding their lives. The visit marked an important step in her work with Women for Women International, an organisation supporting women survivors of war through education, financial skills and community support.How Sophie Turner’s Game of Thrones role led her to RwandaTurner's involvement with women's rights grew partly from the reaction to a controversial storyline in Game of Thrones. Her character, Sansa Stark, experienced sexual violence during the fifth season, and the scene prompted considerable criticism from viewers. However, Turner believed the public response revealed something important about the way sexual violence was discussed.In an interview reported by Arab News in March 2017, the actress said she was shocked by the reaction. She questioned why audiences considered the depiction of rape on television unacceptable while sexual violence continued to affect women around the world. Turner argued that such experiences deserved attention rather than being treated as subjects too uncomfortable to discuss.The conversation prompted her to use her public profile to raise awareness of gender-based violence. Women for Women International says that researching and filming the rape and abuse scenes inspired Turner to support survivors of sexual violence.Her interest eventually led her to Rwanda, where the legacy of mass violence was still shaping women’s lives decades after the genocide.The devastating legacy of Rwanda's 1994 genocideThe 1994 genocide against the Tutsi remains one of the darkest periods in Rwanda's history. Women for Women International states that more than one million people were killed during approximately 100 days of violence.Sexual violence was also widespread. The organisation estimates that between 100,000 and 250,000 women were raped during the genocide, while the United Nations estimates of up to 500,000 women subjected to systematic rape.The consequences extended far beyond the immediate violence. Many women lost husbands, relatives and homes, while others were left responsible for supporting children and surviving family members. The genocide also transformed Rwanda's population and workforce, with women accounting for around 70% of the population in its aftermath.Women for Women International began working in Rwanda in 1997, three years after the genocide, to help women recover and regain control over their lives.What did Sophie Turner witness during her visitDuring her trip, Turner met women who had survived the genocide and were participating in programmes run by Women for Women International. The organisation explains that she saw how survivors were receiving practical support to move beyond survival and towards greater independence.The actress encountered women whose progress illustrated the difference that financial training and community support could make. One of them was Grace, a single mother of five who had struggled to provide for her children after losing her husband.According to Women for Women International, Grace learnt saving skills through a women's opportunity centre. The knowledge helped her provide for her children and eventually purchase two cows, giving her family greater financial security.Turner also met Judith, a woman who had established her own textiles business. Judith made clothes while teaching other women the skills she had developed, allowing her work to benefit people beyond her own household.How Women for Women International helps survivors rebuildWomen for Women International focuses on helping women affected by conflict become economically independent and participate more actively in their communities. Its work in Rwanda began in 1997 and has continued through programmes designed to strengthen women's financial security, confidence and rights.The organisation describes its Stronger Women, Stronger Nations programme as a combination of peer support and practical training. Participants learn how to generate income, save money and become financially independent while gaining knowledge about their rights.The programme also encourages women to participate in decisions within their households and communities.The organisation reported that 68% of women involved in its programme participated in household spending decisions, compared with 49% when they enrolled. Participation in savings and self-help groups also increased, while more women took leadership roles in community groups.In 2021, local leadership established Women for Women Rwanda as an independent sister organisation. The country profile states that the programme had reached more than 82,418 women since its office opened in 1997, including 811 women and girls enrolled in programmes in 2025.Sophie Turner became an ambassador for survivorsTurner's visit was followed by a formal role with Women for Women International. On International Women's Day in 2017, she announced that she had become an ambassador for the organisation, according to its official profile.Her responsibilities included using her public platform to raise awareness about women survivors of war and help bring attention to their experiences. The organisation's ambassador programme relies on public figures to communicate its mission, mobilise resources and encourage wider support for women rebuilding their lives after conflict.Arab News, reporting in March 2017, described Turner as a new patron of the charity.You use AI every day. articles.title: An Indiana security guard was struck by a car carrying suspected phone thieves outside a hospital in 2017; nine years later, an appeals court has revived his negligence claim over missing barriers
articles.summary: An Indiana appeals court has revived a security guard's negligence case against Indiana University Health (IU Health) after he was struck by a car outside
articles.body: An Indiana appeals court has revived a security guard's negligence case against Indiana University Health (IU Health) after he was struck by a car outside a hospital in Indianapolis in 2017. Paul McGann was injured when two suspected phone thieves drove into him while fleeing the hospital parking lot. He had accused the hospital of failing to install or maintain speed bumps and barricades that could have prevented vehicles from hitting pedestrians. On November 6, the court overturned a lower court's decision in favour of the hospital and sent the case back for further proceedings.According to details of the case available on Justia, the incident took place on August 9, 2017, at IU Health Methodist Hospital. McGann, who was a police officer, was working off-duty as a security guard at the hospital. He was employed through Calvert Asset & Property Protection, a subcontractor of the security company hired by IU Health.The trouble began when a woman reported that two people had stolen her phone in the hospital's emergency department parking lot. Hospital police officers reached the spot and approached the suspects as their car was pulling out of a parking space.The officers asked them to stop and questioned them about the stolen phone. McGann also arrived at the scene and stood in front of their car. The vehicle suddenly accelerated, hit him and sped away. McGann suffered injuries.Security guard sued the hospitalIn August 2019, McGann filed a negligence case against IU Health. He argued that the hospital was responsible for keeping its premises reasonably safe for people visiting or working there.He alleged that the hospital had failed to maintain speed bumps or barricades that could stop vehicles from hitting pedestrians. He also accused it of failing to keep the property reasonably safe.McGann initially included James Calvert, who owned the security firm, in the lawsuit. He alleged that Calvert had failed to provide the required training, equipment and insurance. However, Calvert was later removed from the case.In November 2025, IU Health asked the trial court to dismiss the case without a full trial. The hospital argued that it had no responsibility to control the people who were fleeing after the reported phone theft.McGann opposed the request. He said the hospital had focused on the wrong issue. His complaint was not just about whether the hospital should have controlled the suspects. He had also accused it of failing to maintain speed bumps and barricades in the parking lot.He argued that these allegations concerned the safety of the hospital premises and needed to be considered separately.The hospital maintained that McGann had not provided evidence showing that speed bumps or barricades would have prevented the accident. The trial court eventually ruled in favour of IU Health without giving a detailed explanation. McGann then challenged that decision before the Indiana Court of Appeals.Why the appeals court overturned the decisionThe appeals court examined the arguments made by both sides and found that the hospital had not properly addressed McGann's claim about the parking lot's safety.The court explained that property owners have a responsibility to take reasonable steps to protect people on their premises from risks they could foresee.It also pointed out that McGann's complaint specifically mentioned missing speed bumps and barricades. This meant his allegation concerned the physical condition of the hospital's property.However, IU Health's request to dismiss the case had focused only on whether it was responsible for controlling the suspects who drove away. The hospital had not directly challenged the allegation about the missing barriers.The court said the hospital first needed to address that claim before expecting McGann to produce evidence in response.It also examined the police report and supplementary report submitted by IU Health. These documents described how McGann was struck by the car but did not provide details about the parking lot's layout or condition.As a result, the reports did not establish that the hospital's parking area was reasonably safe or disprove McGann's allegation.The hospital later argued that McGann had failed to show how speed bumps or barricades could have prevented his injuries. However, the appeals court said IU Health could not raise this issue for the first time in its reply after McGann had already responded to its original request.The court said a person responding to such a request must be allowed to address the arguments actually raised by the other side.The Indiana Court of Appeals concluded that the hospital had not properly challenged McGann's allegation about the condition of its premises. It therefore overturned the earlier decision in IU Health's favour. The case has now been sent back to the lower court for further proceedings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Mehul Choksi speaks for first time from Antwerp prison, calls allegations against him a ‘conspiracy’
articles.summary: LONDON: Fugitive diamond businessman Mehul Choksi has given an interview to an investigative “Daily Mail” podcast from prison in Antwerp, where he is
articles.body: LONDON: Fugitive diamond businessman Mehul Choksi has given an interview to an investigative “Daily Mail” podcast from prison in Antwerp, where he is fighting extradition to India, saying that all the allegations against him “are a conspiracy”.“It was the govt of India that wanted to make me a scapegoat. It was a conspiracy. It was banks misreporting internal figures in the systems for many years. There was nothing else in it. They wanted to place the blame. They set this up and they made the country collapse,” Choksi, who looked gaunt and frail, claimed to Mail reporters in the visitors’ room with armed guards and security cameras, in episode 5 of the series “Heists, Scams and Lies: The Billion Dollar Honey Trap”.Launched by the Mail’s Crime Desk this week, it explores his alleged $1.8 million Punjab National Bank fraud and his allegations of being kidnapped in Antigua in a “state-sanctioned honeytrap plot”.The Mail was not allowed to carry in dictaphones or pen and paper, but scribbled down what he said using crayons and paper from a kids’ colouring set they found inside the jail.He said he had had PTSD since his alleged kidnap in Antigua. “I have a lot of mental pressure and anxiety,” he said, adding he “sees the kidnappers all the time” in prison and “dreamt they are coming to get him”. He works in a mince factory inside the prison and his family come to see him most days and in the evenings he “does a lot of cooking”, he said.“I was kidnapped and brought from Antigua to Dominica and I was jailed. You can see I was forcibly brought. I do realise that to fight against the state is not easy. I am sure one day the real truth will come out and God will be kinder,” Choksi said, adding his story was “like a movie” and he trusted the justice system to free him.He said it was “horrible” his kidnappers, who he claims were agents for India, had walked free and he was locked up. The podcast tracks some of them down and they all deny the allegations. He also left the Mail’s questions about the PNB scam “largely unanswered”.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: David Walliams accused of sexual misconduct in Guardian and ITN investigation
articles.summary: ITN and the Guardian allege the comedian preyed on teenage girls and young women. He has denied all allegations.
articles.body:
ITV News and the Guardian have published reports alleging that David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including one who was aged 15.

The allegations were made as a part of a joint three-year investigation by the two news organisations, which was published after the entertainer lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public.

Some of the women accuse Walliams of "grooming" them when they were teenagers. One now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15-years- old as a "sexual assault".

In a letter to journalists published by the Guardian, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

He said he "realised that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with" and said he regretted not always taking "people's feelings properly into account".

If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

Walliams shot to fame alongside Matt Lucas in the early 2000s with BBC sketch comedy Little Britain, and also served as a judge on ITV's Britain's Got Talent and launched a best-selling series of children's books.

The Guardian and ITV News say that several of the women, who do not know one another, allege they were targets of unwanted sexual advances from Walliams.

One woman alleges she met Walliams at a fan event when she was 15. She says he groomed her and they had sex when she was 17

Another woman alleges she met Walliams for a coffee when she was 15, before going back to his house where he allegedly tried to lift up her shirt and commit an act that she now describes as a sexual assault

A woman who worked as a model in her teens accused Walliams of grooming her. A different woman who also worked as a model said Walliams tried to kiss her while showing her around his home

The investigation claimed Walliams had a sexual relationship with at least one junior employee at publisher HarperCollins, and pursued another

Other women allege inappropriate behaviour at ITV's Britain's Got Talent, such as inviting girls and young women to his dressing room

In a letter addressed to journalists working on the ITV and Guardian investigation, Walliams wrote: "Looking back, I realise that at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with.

"I realise I did not always take people's feelings properly into account. That is something I regret. And whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something that I never did."

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

After the investigation was published on Tuesday, Walliams's long-time literary agent Independent Talent Group confirmed it had dropped him.

A BBC spokesperson described the allegations as "serious" and the corporation has removed Little Britain from BBC iPlayer.

Sky also described the allegations as "extremely serious", saying it was dropping its upcoming adaptation of Walliams's fantasy feature Fing! and had "already removed content which features him from our platforms".

The Metropolitan Police said it has contacted the Guardian and ITV News to "to ensure that any potential victims" are "made aware of how they could report any criminal allegations to police".

One of the women who alleged Walliams "groomed" her as a teenager told BBC Newsnight she was "angry" at his behaviour.

Lilly Creightmore - who Walliams contacted when she was 18 - waived her right to anonymity.

Creightmore told Newsnight that a month after they first met, Walliams told her she "could move in with him and basically that I could be his flatmate".

She said that after she arrived to stay at his house she "felt instantly pressured to share a bed with him".

"In the evenings, he would sort of come and sit with me and stroke my leg, and one night I think he put his head in my lap and sort of be like, 'are you sure you don't want to come and sleep in my bed with me?' I had an inner strength like, 'no I'm not attracted to you in that way'... I felt I was being manipulated," she added.

She told Newsnight: "I am angry, I'm suppressing it well, but just that this culture of older men in positions of power needs to go, needs to stop. They're abusing their positions, using young people and abusing young people, and people of any age of course. There were too many men in power still, that are doing this and they need to go."

Walliams's lawyers told the ITV News and Guardian investigation that he denied grooming Creightmore or acting inappropriately. They added he did not "target" her because she was "vulnerable" or "young".

Walliams said he believed his friendship with Lilly was a "special one" and felt "devastated" by her account. He denied the offers of help or gifts were attempts to groom, manipulate or coerce her into sleeping with him.

Two women, given pseudonyms of Alex and Jade in the investigation, have alleged that they first had contact with Walliams when they were 15 years old.

Alex alleged that she met Walliams in 2004 at a fan event when she was 15. She claimed that she and Walliams stayed in touch over the next two years and they had consensual sex for the first time when she was 17, the report alleged.

Asked how she feels about Walliams now, she told the investigation: "I think I was groomed. 100%."

Walliams told the publications he believed she was 18 at the time they had sex. The investigation said Alex had joked to Walliams in an email she was "old enough to go drinking", but was actually 17.

Walliams denied grooming Alex. He said he is "mortified to learn" that their "brief, consensual relationship has caused her sadness".

Jade also alleged she met Walliams when she was 15, in August 2007, in a Soho cafe.

Later, at his home, she alleged, he kissed her, lifted up her T-shirt, went on to commit an act that she now characterises as a sexual assault, and tried to put her hand down his trousers. She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

She said she considers what she says happened to her to have been "grooming", adding: "It's completely wrong in every way."

Walliams strongly denied that he had any sexual contact with Jade. He said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and says he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

Another woman, named as Ella, says she was 19 and working as a model when she rejected Walliams when he tried to kiss her during a tour of his home.

She referred to what happened that night as "unwanted physical touching and emotional manipulation".

Walliams said he made a "clumsy pass" at Ella, and he made no further approaches. He said he had no intention of intimidating Ella, or making her feel uncomfortable.

Other women claimed they were invited to Walliams's dressing room at Britain's Got Talent, or contacted by him after attending a taping.

Syco Entertainment, the company that created Britain's Got Talent, said it had had "no knowledge of the allegations described and was not made aware of them at the time".

The show's production company, Fremantle UK, said "no complaint has ever been made" against Walliams and encouraged anyone who "feels they have been the subject of any impropriety or wrongdoing by anyone... to come forward".

Women who worked for publisher HarperCollins also allege Walliams behaved inappropriately towards younger female employees.

One intern at the company told colleagues she had had a consensual sexual relationship with Walliams, but felt it was an "abuse of power".

After conducting an internal investigation, HarperCollins announced it was dropping Walliams as an author. Earlier this year, it also said it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue.

In a statement responding to ITV News and the Guardian's investigation, the company said it takes employee wellbeing "extremely seriously".

Walliams denies that he sexually harassed anyone at HarperCollins or behaved inappropriately in the workplace.

Walliams, 55, previously brought legal action against Independent Television News (ITN), which makes ITV News, and Guardian News and Media (GNM), publisher of the Guardian, to try and prevent the claims being published.

The two news organisations had argued that they believed it was in the public interest to publish the allegations.

Walliams denied the claims and his lawyers said any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself, after two previous suicide attempts, and that the court should prevent any publication or broadcast.

Last week, a High Court judge rejected the injunction request and Walliams did not lodge an appeal, clearing the way for him to be named.

articles.title: Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM Sheikh Hasina's supporters stage protest
articles.summary: Supporters of Sheikh Hasina want her to return from exile in India.
articles.body:
Police in Bangladesh have fired tear gas and rubber bullets to disperse supporters of the deposed Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who are demanding her return to the country.

A police vehicle was set on fire in Gopalganj district, where the banned student wing of Hasina's Awami League party clashed with security forces.

Nationwide protests by pro-Hasina activists started a day after the former leader said she had requested a passport to return to Bangladesh from exile in India.

The demonstrations by the student wing, called Bangladesh Chhatra League (BCL), are seen as the first organised show of force by Hasina's supporters since she was ousted in August 2024 following a huge uprising against her rule .

Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.

Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.

A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.

Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.

Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.

"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.

"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.

Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.

Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.

The United Nations has estimated up to 1,400 people were killed , most by gunfire from security forces, during the anti-government protests in 2024.

The activities of the Awami League were banned soon after she fled the country and it was not allowed to contest the February general election.

A special Bangladeshi tribunal last year sentenced her to death in absentia after being found guilty of crimes against humanity.

She has denied all the charges, calling the trial "biased and politically motivated".

Despite the death penalty threat, Hasina said she wanted to return to Bangladesh in December and requesteded the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to issue her with a passport.

But the Bangladeshi government said the country would not provide a passport to her and called her "a terrorist".

"She is a fugitive criminal. We have an active extradition treaty with India. We want her handed over," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's junior foreign affairs minister, said.

"Should we treat her like an ordinary commercial traveller and tell her to come and visit her in-laws' residence?" Kobir asked.

A state prosecutor in Bangladesh on Tuesday said the verdict would be executed if she came back, saying she had missed the opportunity to appeal.

Awami League leaders allege that in the past two years hundreds of supporters have been killed in mob violence and dozens have died in the custody of security forces.

Dhaka officials reject accusations that Awami League supporters are being systematically targeted.

articles.title: Joe Biden addresses critics who said he hid his stage 4 cancer diagnosis in upcoming memoir
articles.summary: Former President Joe Biden's responded to critics who accused him of hiding his stage 4 prostate cancer diagnosis from the public in his new book, "Promise Me, America."
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden responded to accusations that he concealed his cancer diagnosis during his presidency in his new book, according to parts of an excerpt published Tuesday. The former president was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had spread to his bones in May 2025. "What did surprise me was the cynical twist the story took in the political press and among political commentators," Biden wrote in his upcoming memoir, according to MS NOW. "Almost immediately, the reaction was: ‘You hid it from us.’ ‘You must have known it.’ ‘You’re lying.’ Let me tell you something: There isn’t anyone in this world with stage 4 cancer who doesn’t wish it had been caught sooner." JIMMY FALLON SWIPES AT BIDEN’S UPCOMING MEMOIR, JOKES KAMALA HARRIS WROTE THE END OF IT The memoir, titled "Promise Me, America," is set to be released on Nov. 17. Biden reflects on his four years in the White House in the book, covering the COVID-19 pandemic, the aftermath of the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, domestic legislation, global diplomacy and his decision to run for re-election before later stepping aside in 2024. The memoir also details the personal deliberations behind his decision to end his 2024 re-election bid. "For anyone to think I would try to ignore or hide a cancer ravaging my body is absurd," Biden wrote, according to the excerpt. "Here are the simple facts. Standard medical protocol is to stop testing men for prostate cancer after the age of seventy." Biden said Sunday that he would not be able to participate in as many conversations about his book as he had hoped because of his treatment. "Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me," he said. "But sometimes it slows me down. What that means is, unfortunately, I won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped. However, I’m hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves." "In the daily grind of the White House, it could be difficult to step back and take the long view — because so much was happening every minute," Biden wrote in his book, according to the excerpt. "But now, from my lake house, I am able to slow down and savor the results of my Presidency." JILL BIDEN SAYS FORMER PRESIDENT WILL LIVE WITH STAGE 4 CANCER 'FOR THE REST OF HIS LIFE,' HAS SLOWED DOWN Biden's memoir comes after several books about the 2024 election shed light on the Biden administration's decision-making leading up to the election, including former Vice President Kamala Harris' "107 Days," released in 2025. Harris' book focused mostly on her short campaign for the presidency, but also included some insight into her relationship with Biden and his team. Harris wrote that she felt her decision to remain silent about Biden's 2024 re-election bid had been reckless. "'It’s Joe and Jill’s decision.' We all said that, like a mantra, as if we’d all been hypnotized. Was it grace, or was it recklessness? In retrospect, I think it was recklessness," she said. "The stakes were simply too high. This wasn’t a choice that should have been left to an individual’s ego, an individual’s ambition. It should have been more than a personal decision." articles.title: Matthew Farwell convicted in the 2021 deaths of Sandra Birchmore and her unborn baby
articles.summary: Former Massachusetts police officer Matthew Farwell was found guilty on Tuesday of 2021 killing Sandra Birchmore and causing the death of her unborn child.
articles.body: Former Massachusetts police officer Matthew Farwell was found guilty on Tuesday of 2021 killing Sandra Birchmore and causing the death of her unborn child. Farwell was found guilty on Tuesday of both counts he faced on the second full day of deliberations. Birchmore was pregnant at the time of her death, on Feb. 1, 2021, and she and Farwell had been in an extramarital relationship — Stoughton police have said it began when Birchmore was 15 and enrolled in the department’s police explorer program. Farwell faced federal charges of killing a witness or victim and of violating a federal law protecting unborn children. He’s pleaded not guilty, and his attorneys have argued that Birchmore did in fact die by suicide. The jury began deliberating on Friday, the 19th day of the trial, which was held in Boston’s federal court. It featured testimony from Farwell’s twin brother, who admitted having extramarital sex with Birchmore when she was an adult and acknowledged that he’s been given immunity in exchange for testifying. Farwell declined to take the stand in his defense. Birchmore’s death at her Canton apartment was initially ruled a suicide, but new scrutiny was placed on the case in 2022, when Stoughton’s chief of police held a news conference to reveal that three former officers had inappropriate sexual relationships with the young woman, one when she was a girl, and that the officers, including the Farwell brothers, resigned during the investigation. The revelation came as defense attorneys for Karen Read were making their own initial police misconduct claims in her now-well-known case, which also involved the town of Canton and the Norfolk County District Attorney’s Office. Some of her supporters went on to advocate for Birchmore’s death to be re-investigated. In 2024, Farwell was arrested and federal prosecutors announced that the former officer had been indicted after an FBI investigation. They alleged that he killed Birchmore to keep her from revealing their relationship and the alleged crimes connected to it. “Sandra Birchmore survived years of grooming, statutory rape and then sexual violence, all at the hands of Matthew Farwell, who was employed throughout the relationship as an officer and then detective for the Stoughton Police Department,” said Joshua Leavy, then the acting U.S. attorney for Massachusetts, at a news conference at the time. Farwell isn’t charged with murder in his trial because murder is, with a few exceptions, prosecuted by the state the death took place in. He hasn’t been charged in state court; the Norfolk District Attorney’s Office’s has referred to the case as “an ongoing and pending criminal matter,” which limits what the agency can say about it. Birchmore’s estate has filed a civil lawsuit against the Town of Stoughton, Farwell and others; it’s set for a hearing after the federal trial ends. “There’s a lot more work to do,” Barbara Wright, Birchmore’s cousin, said outside the courthouse. “We’re not done.” “There are still other people to hold accountable, who enabled him, people who looked the other way,” Wright said. The case has continued to roil Stoughton — its police chief and town manager are both on leave amid an outside investigation into Chief Donna McNamara’s claim that Town Manager Thomas Calter tried to force her out of the job. Her lawsuit alleges that Calter had told her to destroy a second internal investigation about the case, which she’s denied doing. Farwell will be sentenced on Feb. 3, 2027, six years and two days after Birchmore was killed.

articles.title: 15 lakh visit Ayodhya in a week, homestays cash in on Deepotsav rush
articles.summary: Ayodhya drew 15 lakh visitors Nov 1–7 during Deepotsav, nearly doubling last year; Ram Lalla temple visits hit 10 lakh, boosting homestay occupancy.
articles.body: Lucknow/Ayodhya: Ayodhya received around 15 lakh visitors between Nov 1 and 7 this year, according to official data released by the state govt on Tuesday.The figure is nearly double the footfall recorded during the corresponding period last year.The surge in tourist arrivals during the Deepotsav week also translated into a sharp rise in business for local homestays, with several reporting full occupancy and extended bookings.Visits to the Ram Lalla temple also doubled during the seven-day period, rising from over five lakh in 2025 to around 10 lakh this year, according to tourism department figures.The increased footfall brought guests from across the country and abroad to local homestays, creating business and employment opportunities for local families.Several properties reported occupancy levels of 80% to 100%, while some owners said they had to turn away visitors due to a shortage of rooms.Poonam Sonkar, who runs Poonam Homestay, reported nearly 80% occupancy, with several guests extending their stays. The growth has also helped her family retain its younger generation in the business. Her son turned down a job offer in a major city in Rajasthan to join the family enterprise, which now provides employment to two people.“Today, our business is growing, and my son is earning through the work we have built here. He no longer needs to move to a big city in search of employment,” Sonkar said.Vasudev Maurya of Shri Ramdoot Niwas Homestay reported a 120-130% increase in business compared with normal days, with all rooms occupied. Guests, particularly from Maharashtra, stayed longer and opted for home-cooked meals. Rooms were available for Rs 1,000-1,200 a day, making homestays an affordable alternative to hotels, he said.At Kusum Homestay, Avinash Kusum said rooms remained occupied throughout the festive period, with visitors appreciating home-cooked meals and the family atmosphere.Praveen Mishra of Shri Shivay Homestay also reported 100% occupancy and said he had to turn away tourists when rooms ran out.Raj Kumari Tiwari, who runs The Rama Junction (B&B), said the property was fully occupied during Deepotsav, hosting visitors from Kerala and Tamil Nadu. The business has become an important source of family income after her husband’s retirement from the Army.Tourism and culture minister Jaiveer Singh said, “The growing response to Ayodhya’s homestays reflects how tourism is creating new income and employment opportunities for local families.”Additional chief secretary and director general (tourism) Amrit Abhijat said homestays were becoming an important part of Ayodhya’s tourism ecosystem, offering visitors a more personal experience while generating livelihood opportunities for local households.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news. articles.title: US soldier arrested in UK on suspicion of spying for Russia
articles.summary: London Metropolitan Police says its ‘counterterror’ forces worked closely with the FBI and US military to make arrest.
articles.body:
An unidentified member of the United States military has been arrested in the United Kingdom on suspicion of carrying out espionage for Russia, according to British authorities.

The 41-year-old was arrested on Tuesday near Gloucester in southwest England on suspicion of violating two sections of the National Security Act 2023 – for assisting a foreign intelligence service and obtaining or disclosing protected information, London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement.

The police said its “counterterror” forces worked closely with the FBI and US military.

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, the UK’s senior national coordinator for “counterterrorism” policing, said that this is a “significant arrest and investigation” and that the allegations are “serious and our investigation is very much ongoing”.

The US’s FBI Director Kash Patel also called it an “important arrest”, dealing with allegations of espionage that are of “utmost concern” for the US and its allies.

“This FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners,” Patel said.

Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of the US Army Counterintelligence Command, said: “This case demonstrates the strength of our partnerships and the resolve of the counterintelligence community.”

Officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire. The man remains in custody at a London ‌police station, police said.

Police said the arrest was not related to other “counterterror” investigations, indicating it was not connected with a suspected plot linked to Iran in September at the British Royal Air Force base near Gloucester, RAF Fairford , that hosts the US Air Force.

After the threat, the US Air Force withdrew bombers that had been used to strike Iran during the Middle East conflict from RAF Fairford.

articles.title: Spain's king and queen attend memorial service for rail crash victims
articles.summary: Sixty-nine people died in the collision near Toledo two weeks ago and 28 are still in hospital.
articles.body:
Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train crash.

The accident occurred when one train, travelling at high speed, ploughed into the back of another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line, near the small town of Urda, about 40 miles from Toledo.

It was the worst rail tragedy in Spain since 2013. Twenty-eight people remain in hospital.

"The tragic accident in Urda has left our families, our towns and our society with a pain that is difficult to accept," Archbishop Cerro Chaves told those present.

Representatives of those killed carried lit candles to the front of the cathedral and placed them next to the main altar. The first reading of the service was by Ana Benítez, sister of David Benítez, a 38-year-old father-of-two who died.

The king and queen were met with applause by bystanders as they entered the cathedral and at the end of the service, after Catholic Mass, they spoke to relatives of the victims.

Senior politicians also attended the service, including the leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano García-Page, and Transport and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo.

Cuerpo took on the transport portfolio following the resignation last week of Óscar Puente from the post.

Puente had come under mounting pressure following the crash, Spain's second major rail tragedy this year after 46 people died in a collision on the same high-speed line in January.

Some local people from the town of Adamuz in Andalusia, where that accident happened, as well as residents of Urda, were present for the memorial service.

The investigation into the recent accident is still in progress. Puente suggested that human error combined with a glitch in the safety system may have been the cause.

The tragedy happened a month before the 29 November general election and is seen as likely to hurt Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's attempts to secure re-election.

The ceremony took place on the same day as a nationwide strike by train drivers, who are demanding greater safety on the rail network.

Rail services were also expected to be affected across the country on Wednesday due to a general strike, led by housing activists calling for urgent measures to control rental costs.
